Measure EE includes Council information and investigation powers and authorizes an independent budget and legislative analyst office. Councilmembers would retain the right to seek information and follow up on service requests. These provisions could help the Council scrutinize city decisions.

Measure EE would change how the mayor, Council, and City Administrator share responsibility for running Oakland. This overview includes the new executive powers and the oversight provisions supporters point to.

Measure EE would keep a City Administrator. Finance and Human Resources would be the Administrator’s guaranteed departments, and the mayor could assign additional departments. The mayor would direct the Administrator and could remove them after advising Council.

Measure EE would make the mayor Oakland’s chief executive officer and give the office broad responsibility for managing city departments. Most permanent department-head appointments would not require Council confirmation. That would move substantial administrative and personnel authority to an elected political office.

Measure EE would make the mayor the chief executive, but not require the mayor to attend council meetings. The City Administrator would be relegated to overseeing just a handful of departments (Finance, HR, IT), leaving the City Council - and the public - without answers to pressing questions about what's going on behind closed doors. The public deserves to be able to hear from their highest elected official and hold them to account.

Measure EE would make the mayor the chief executive, but would allow the mayor to attend Council and committee meetings through a designee, unless excused. The City Administrator could also meet the Council attendance requirement through a designee.

Measure EE would not legalize bribery or other unlawful conduct. Our concern is that reducing checks on appointments would create more opportunities for abuse. We do not believe the proposal strikes the right balance between executive leadership, professional administration, and independent oversight.

Measure EE would preserve the eight-member Council and remove the mayor’s current tie-breaking vote. The mayor would gain a veto over most Council resolutions and ordinances, with specified exceptions. Overriding most vetoes would require six of eight Councilmembers; budget vetoes have a separate process.

Measure EE would still require Council confirmation for the City Administrator and permanent heads of Human Resources, Finance, and specified infrastructure departments. Civil-service protections and other Charter exceptions would remain.
